title: Charlie and Dee Find Love

jokes.text: Charlie barking like a dog to scare off a would-be bike thief for the Waitress
jokes.setup: Charlie has been stalking the Waitress and is watching her bike to protect her; a man approaches the unlocked bike
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response to the threat is to bark like a dog and yell 'Keep it moving, guy!'
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's perfectly in character — Charlie's feral, childlike quality expressed through literal dog behavior while performing a 'heroic' act of protection. The juxtaposition of the sincere stalker dedication with the animal method is rich. High character integration because only Charlie does this.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I just... I can't believe you just bought, like, another ridiculous ugly car.

jokes.text: Charlie lists the insane 'helpful' things he does for the Waitress: putting vitamins in her shampoo so her hair doesn't fall out, testing her food so it doesn't get poisoned
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to justify his stalking by claiming he does helpful things for the Waitress
jokes.punchline: The 'helpful' acts are themselves deeply creepy forms of stalking and violation — secretly dosing her shampoo and tasting her food
jokes.explanation: This is exceptionally well-crafted because each item on Charlie's list reframes his obsession as 'care' while being objectively horrifying. The escalating specificity (vitamins in shampoo, food testing) reveals the depth of his delusion with perfect deadpan delivery. It plants a crucial plot seed (the rat poison callback) and is 100% Charlie-specific. Scores 8+ because it's character-defining, structurally elegant, and darkly funny with real wit behind the horror.

dialogue.speaker: Sweet Dee
dialogue.line: You are lucky I am letting you into my goddamn... Oh, shit, okay, okay, here she comes

jokes.text: Charlie's completely flat, deflated 'Yeah, I hear you. It's... Okay.' after the Waitress delivers a passionate speech telling him to leave her alone forever
jokes.setup: The Waitress delivers an emotionally charged ultimatum demanding Charlie leave her alone permanently
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response is completely flat and unfazed — 'Yeah, I hear you. It's... Okay.' — as if she's told him the weather
jokes.explanation: The deflation of the Waitress's passionate speech by Charlie's total non-reaction is a classic Sunny beat. His inability to register the gravity of the situation is perfect character work. The trailing '...Okay' is particularly good — it suggests he's already half-checked out mentally.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Charlie barking at potential bike thief

jokes.text: Dee says she doesn't want to go back to the bar — she'd rather keep following the Waitress around
jokes.setup: Charlie has just been told to stop stalking the Waitress and seems to accept it; he asks to go back to the bar
jokes.punchline: Dee, who was just lecturing Charlie about the Waitress rejecting him, immediately reveals she also wants to keep stalking her
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat that reveals Dee's hypocrisy — she's just as low as Charlie. Economical and character-specific but not particularly inspired. Works as a grace note.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I keep a list of things that I do, okay? I watch your bike so it doesn't get stolen, okay? I put, uh... I put vitamins in your shampoo so your hair doesn't fall out. I test your food so it doesn't get poisoned.

jokes.text: Dee's reaction to nearly being hit by Trevor's car transforms instantly from murderous rage ('I am gonna smash your teeth into dust!') to stunned attraction the moment she sees him
jokes.setup: Dee is screaming death threats at the driver who nearly hit her car
jokes.punchline: She sees Trevor and goes completely silent mid-threat — 'Oh... look at you. My God.'
jokes.explanation: Classic hard pivot from aggression to attraction, efficiently executed. The specific threat about smashing teeth to dust makes the deflation funnier. Good economy — the joke lands in a single beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Mm, no, I'd like to follow her around.

jokes.text: Extended awkward silence / reaction beat as Charlie and Ruby stare at each other after being introduced — culminating in nervous laughter from everyone
jokes.setup: Ruby says 'Hi' to Charlie after Trevor introduces them
jokes.punchline: Dead silence. Then more silence. Then everyone nervously laughs. Then Dee actually gags.
jokes.explanation: The long beat of silence followed by Dee's physical gag is a solid visual/physical comedy moment. Dee gagging at the prospect of Charlie being with an attractive woman is mean-spirited in the best Sunny way. Works better on screen than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Sweet Dee
dialogue.line: If you don't have car insurance, you better have dental because I am gonna smash your teeth into dust!

jokes.text: Sweet Dee gags/retches audibly at the sight of Charlie potentially connecting with an attractive woman
jokes.setup: Charlie and Ruby are having a sweet awkward moment
jokes.punchline: Dee's body physically rejects the idea — she audibly gags
jokes.explanation: One sound effect that says everything. Dee's contempt for Charlie expressed as a physical reflex is very Sunny. The economy is perfect — maximum disdain, minimum words.

dialogue.speaker: TREVOR
dialogue.line: So sorry, that was completely my fault.

dialogue.speaker: SWEET DEE
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's goddamn your fault, I... Oh... look at you. My God.

jokes.text: Mac recounts that his uncle 'drowned' in a vat of molten steel at TaftCo, then corrects himself that he 'burned up'
jokes.setup: Mac is bragging about his family's connection to TaftCo Enterprises
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions his uncle died in their molten steel — then semantically corrects 'drowned' to 'burned up' as if that's the important distinction to make
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: (1) the horrifying casual mention of an uncle burning to death in corporate molten steel, and (2) the correction that he 'burned up' not 'drowned' — treating the method of death as the important clarification while the death itself is treated as a fun connection. Frank's matter-of-fact 'He didn't drown, he burned up' makes it even better. Dark, economical, and very Sunny. Near 8 territory for how neatly it delivers both the dark premise and the pedantic follow-up.

jokes.text: Dennis's tirade: 'Do not be yourself. Be anybody but yourselves. Anybody!'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee plan to 'just be themselves' on the date with the wealthy Tafts
jokes.punchline: Dennis, without hesitation, tells them this is a catastrophic idea — 'Be anybody but yourselves. Anybody!'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's contempt for Charlie and Dee combined with his narcissistic self-awareness that they are disasters as people is well-expressed. 'Anybody' is the right word — the absoluteness of it is funny. Classic Dennis delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: My uncle even drowned in a vat of their molten steel.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He didn't drown, he burned up.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, he probably burned.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, I don't think he drowned.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Charlie, do not eat any cheese or any cheese-like substances. If you see any cheese, you run away from it!'
jokes.setup: Dennis is giving advice about how to behave on the fancy date
jokes.punchline: His specific instruction is to avoid cheese entirely and to physically flee from it — implying Charlie has an uncontrollable cheese addiction that will embarrass everyone
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The escalation from 'don't eat cheese' to 'run away from it' implies Charlie's cheese problem is so severe he cannot be trusted in its vicinity. It's deeply character-specific (Charlie's cheese obsession is established show lore) and the phrasing 'cheese-like substances' is perfect — it shows Dennis has thought about edge cases. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, do not eat any cheese or any cheese-like substances, okay? If you see any cheese, you run away from it!

jokes.text: Dennis to Dee: 'Do not be a drunk, punchy whore, okay, you whore?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is giving date-night instructions
jokes.punchline: His instruction to Dee is essentially a list of her defining personality traits delivered as prohibitions — capped with calling her 'whore' as a matter of fact address
jokes.explanation: The comma-then-'you whore' at the end is what elevates this from a standard insult. Dennis is so contemptuous that the insult becomes his term of address, not even a separate thought. Very Dennis-specific in its cruel precision.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dee, do not be a drunk, punchy whore, okay, you whore?

jokes.text: Charlie's plan for the date: 'I guess we'll become one of them or something'
jokes.setup: Frank has urgently demanded to know 'the plan' for dealing with the wealthy Tafts
jokes.punchline: Charlie's entire strategy, stated with casual confidence, is 'become one of them or something' — a vague non-plan delivered as if it's entirely reasonable
jokes.explanation: Charlie's breezy confidence about an impossible social strategy is funny because of his obliviousness. The 'or something' is the comedic cherry — genuine uncertainty tacked onto an already-absurd plan.

dialogue.speaker: Sweet Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah. Well, I imagine they destroyed many an Indian. Mm. I too sort of have distaste for the Indians, you know? They're savage things. They're nasty, really.

jokes.text: Charlie and Dee attempting to perform as old-money aristocrats, agreeing that Native Americans 'needed to be exterminated' and congratulating the Taft family for it
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee are desperately trying to impress the wealthy Taft family by mirroring their perceived values
jokes.punchline: They escalate from polite agreement to enthusiastically endorsing genocide — 'Right, right, they needed to be exterminated. I mean, you hate to say it, but...' — trying to seem relatable to old money
jokes.explanation: Dark and uncomfortable — the joke is on Charlie and Dee's desperate class aspiration leading them to endorse atrocities, while also satirizing old-money casual racism. The 'you hate to say it, but' construction is perfect, mirroring how such views are actually expressed. It's genuinely dark subversive comedy with a point.

dialogue.line: Well, and I, too, am of a large... um, money-ful family. He, too. Shippers of-of goods and, uh... Services. Builders of... tall... Buildings.

jokes.text: Charlie claims his family were 'shippers of goods and... services. Builders of... tall... buildings.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to claim his own family has aristocratic old-money credentials
jokes.punchline: His fabricated family legacy is comically vague and generic — he can barely fill in the nouns, trailing off with '...tall... buildings'
jokes.explanation: The ellipses are the joke — Charlie's lie crumbling in real time as he runs out of aristocratic vocabulary. 'Tall... buildings' is the perfect landing. Very Charlie-specific in its inability to maintain even a simple fiction.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Charlie sees cheese and has a breakdown despite trying to ignore it

jokes.text: Charlie and Dee both decline drinks at dinner, then Charlie immediately collapses/groans after spotting cheese — they've been following Dennis's rules to the letter
jokes.setup: Dennis told Charlie to avoid cheese at all costs and Dee not to drink
jokes.punchline: They robotically decline drinks ('No, thank you, never will I drink'), then Charlie immediately groans and spasms at the sight of cheese — his cheese compulsion stronger than his willpower
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Dennis's cheese warning works beautifully because it confirms the cheese problem is EXACTLY as severe as Dennis feared. 'Never will I drink' is a funny robot-speak version of Dee following instructions, and Charlie's immediate failure at the cheese rule shows the futility of Dennis trying to manage them.

dialogue.speaker: Sweet Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, shit, that is such a relief because look at this pit stain. I mean, we're, like, totally, like, normal.

jokes.text: Charlie abandons the pretense: 'I'm sorry, I can't do it! I've been eyeing this guy all night long... We've been putting on airs. I know I come across, like, super fancy. I'm not.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to maintain the aristocratic facade but is physically overwhelmed by cheese
jokes.punchline: He announces he 'comes across super fancy' — an objectively absurd self-assessment — while abandoning the pretense to eat cheese
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sincere belief that he 'comes across super fancy' is a great delusion joke. The word 'airs' is perfect — Charlie using the precise term while having zero self-awareness about his own situation.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: This is like Lady Di being plucked from the streets like the trash she was and the trash that Charlie and Dee are.

jokes.text: Trevor and Ruby reveal they're relieved Charlie and Dee aren't blue-blood fancy — 'We like you guys 'cause you aren't anything like the people that we know'
jokes.setup: We've been led to believe Charlie and Dee are disastrously embarrassing themselves
jokes.punchline: Trevor and Ruby say they prefer them precisely because they're NOT fancy — which immediately sets up the dark irony that the gang misreads this as genuine
jokes.explanation: This is the structural pivot of the episode — the reversal that seems like a win but (as Dennis immediately suspects) is actually the setup for humiliation. Good construction but the joke itself isn't especially sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This is a Les Liaisons Dangereuses... Dangerous Liaisons... Cruel Intentions... She's All That? Can't Buy Me Love? Almost any movie made in the late '90s?

jokes.text: Dee immediately shows off a massive pit stain when asked to 'be themselves': 'I mean, we're totally, like, normal. Oh, my God... look at this pit stain!'
jokes.setup: Given permission to drop the act, Dee goes straight to pride in her bodily malfunction
jokes.punchline: She presents her pit stain as evidence of her normality, with apparent pride — 'You like this pit stain? That's nasty, yo!'
jokes.explanation: The 'That's nasty, yo!' self-commentary is a good touch. Dee treating her pit stain as a social lubricant rather than a source of shame fits her character's obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What about Dee?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What, Dee? No, she's constantly being crushed. She'll bounce back, she always does. Or she won't. It doesn't matter. I don't care about that.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Can the girl not smell Charlie? Can the guy not see Dee? Something's fishy.'
jokes.setup: Mac is thrilled the date is going well
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts through the optimism with brutal objectivity — implying Charlie smells bad enough to smell and Dee is visually off-putting enough to be a red flag, and therefore something is wrong
jokes.explanation: Two-part parallel construction — Charlie has a smell problem, Dee has an appearance problem — delivered with perfect economy. The logic 'something's fishy because this shouldn't be working' is both funny and sets up the plot. Dennis being the smart one here is well-used.

dialogue.speaker: Sweet Dee
dialogue.line: No. No. No, not friends. Hobos.

jokes.text: Dennis's 'Les Liaisons Dangereuses' explanation, requiring him to translate down through 'Cruel Intentions,' 'She's All That,' 'Can't Buy Me Love,' and 'almost any movie made in the late '90s'
jokes.setup: Dennis figures out the rich people are playing a manipulation game and references the classic novel/film
jokes.punchline: None of the gang knows what it is, so Dennis has to keep downgrading his reference — from literary classic to '90s teen movie — to find their level
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The escalating reference downgrade is brilliantly structured — Dennis trying to meet the gang at their level by going from 'Les Liaisons Dangereuses' to 'almost any movie made in the late '90s' — and the fact that NONE of them know even Cruel Intentions is the perfect indictment. It's also meta-smart because it names the episode's own plot structure. The 'almost any movie made in the late '90s' catch-all is excellent comedy writing — maximum frustration in minimum words. Scores 8+ for structure, character integration (only Dennis would start at Laclos), and the elegant self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Ruby
dialogue.line: I think you look really pale. Do you need some sunscreen?

jokes.text: On the question of whether Dee will be okay being humiliated: 'What about Dee?' / 'What, Dee? No, she's constantly being crushed. She'll bounce back, she always does. Or she won't. It doesn't matter. I don't care about that.'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains Ruby is toying with Charlie and will crush him — Mac asks about Dee
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses Dee's wellbeing in rapid escalating indifference: 'She'll bounce back... or she won't. It doesn't matter. I don't care about that.'
jokes.explanation: This is a contender for the best line in the episode. The three-step collapse — 'she'll bounce back / or she won't / it doesn't matter' — is perfectly constructed nihilistic comedy. Each clause is funnier than the last, ending on pure sociopathic indifference. 'I don't care about that' as a full stop is the ideal punctuation. It's deeply Dennis-specific (his sociopathy toward Dee) and highly quotable. Scores 8+ because the construction is exceptionally clean and the character work is pitch-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Sweet Dee
dialogue.line: How about I free that big fat snake in your pants and uninhibit myself all over it?

jokes.text: Frank, Mac, and Dennis showing up uninvited to the Taft estate and being labeled 'Hobos' by Dennis himself when Trevor welcomes them
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee try to tell the gang not to come along to the tennis/estate visit
jokes.punchline: Dennis introduces them as 'Hobos' — preemptively self-labeling as low-class to soften the blow, and Trevor invites them in anyway
jokes.explanation: Dennis calling his own friends 'hobos' is a decent self-aware gag, and the casual 'Come on in, the more the merrier' is a nice beat about how the gang's invasion is part of the trap. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I got more of a Catholic thing going on. You know, sort of the hand of God.

jokes.text: Dennis says he'll 'subtly extract' Ruby's plan — but his stated goal pivots immediately to 'Oh yes, I will definitely have her'
jokes.setup: Dennis announces a plan to protect Charlie by playing tennis with Ruby and getting information
jokes.punchline: Within the same breath, his stated mission has become seduction — 'Oh yes, I will definitely have her'
jokes.explanation: The speed of Dennis's self-serving pivot — from 'protect Charlie' to 'I will have her' — perfectly captures his narcissism. The 'Oh yes, I will definitely have her' as a private statement of intent is very Dennis: predatory, overconfident, and completely on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Ruby
dialogue.line: Oh, oh, Waitress. Why didn't you just say that?

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Uh, because my name is not Waitress.

jokes.text: Frank's catastrophic tennis — staying on the wrong side, missing the ball entirely, shot marked only by 'No.' and 'Damn it!'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis are playing doubles tennis against Trevor and Ruby
jokes.punchline: Frank is completely useless — a single flat 'No.' when told to stay on his side, then immediate failure
jokes.explanation: Frank's flat 'No.' refusal to follow instructions is a small but characteristic beat. Physical comedy that relies on the visual of Danny DeVito failing at tennis. Functional but nothing special without the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Putting rat poison in her shampoo. Just gonna make her hair fall out. Crazy.

jokes.text: Dennis removes his shirt during tennis claiming it's 'ridiculously tight' and 'restricting his play' — then presents himself to Ruby asking 'What do you think of what I'm presenting you?'
jokes.setup: Dennis said he wasn't going to hit on Ruby
jokes.punchline: He removes his shirt and explicitly asks her to evaluate 'what I'm presenting you' — framing his body as a commodity for assessment
jokes.explanation: 'What I'm presenting you' is a great line — Dennis's narcissism expressed in transactional language, as if his body is a formal presentation or product. His immediate pivot into seduction mode despite explicit promises not to is 100% Dennis Reynolds and the specific phrasing is memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: There's a girl who lives in this building, and, um, well, she's... she's the love of my life... And I like you so much that before we move any further, I just... I don't know. I had to get that out there, 'cause I think I'm ready to let her go

jokes.text: Ruby responds to Dennis presenting his body by saying she thinks he 'looks really pale' and asking if he needs sunscreen
jokes.setup: Dennis presents his body expecting admiration
jokes.punchline: Ruby's completely clinical response — she's concerned about his skin health, not attracted
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of Dennis's narcissism — the one thing he cannot handle is indifference. 'I haven't had a chance to get a base going' is a great defensive response. The deflation of his ego is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, shut up, bitch! Who the hell is this, Charlie?! She's my girlfriend.

jokes.text: Mac calling Dennis out for hitting on Ruby; Dennis: 'Oh, shit. Okay. No, you're right. Okay, I went into default mode. My bad.'
jokes.setup: Mac confronts Dennis about hitting on Ruby after explicitly promising not to
jokes.punchline: Dennis acknowledges 'default mode' — he has a factory-preset setting that is predatory seduction, which activates without conscious thought
jokes.explanation: 'Default mode' is a genuinely great character-specific phrase — it implies Dennis's predatory behavior is so ingrained it's his neutral state. The casual 'My bad' after a potentially predatory interaction is a perfect Dennis non-apology. Highly quotable as a character-defining moment.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: My uncle's probably built into the foundation of this place.

jokes.text: Dee drunkenly singing Bad Company at the tennis court while everyone watches in horror
jokes.setup: Despite explicit instructions not to drink, the scene cuts to Dee belting out a classic rock song, drunk, at a tennis court
jokes.punchline: Frank screams 'What the hell is she doing?! She's gonna ruin this whole thing!' — the visual of Dee drunk-singing at a formal rich-person event
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Dennis's warning that Dee would drink. The specific choice of Bad Company ('Bad Company' — she is bad company) has a nice double-meaning. Works better visually but Frank's reaction sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Trevor
dialogue.line: Well, you guys'll be out here with some of my frat brothers' guests.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah. We'll... we'll meet you af... we'll see you after.

jokes.text: Drunk Dee to Trevor: 'How about I free that big fat snake in your pants and uninhibit myself all over it?' followed by a belch
jokes.setup: Trevor says he loves how 'free and uninhibited' Dee is
jokes.punchline: Dee takes the compliment as a sexual invitation and delivers an aggressively crude come-on about his 'snake,' then immediately belches
jokes.explanation: The pivot from Trevor's genuinely sweet comment to Dee's aggressively vulgar response is well-timed, and the word 'uninhibit' used as a verb applied to herself is creative. The belch punctuation is perfect Dee. The joke earns its crudeness through the juxtaposition.

dialogue.speaker: Sweet Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, no, Mac. I see what's going on here. He's doing to us what I like to do to Charlie and the waitress.

jokes.text: Mac's fighting stance/near-attack on Trevor; Trevor asks if Mac is trained, and Mac claims Krav Maga, Judo, Karate while Frank claims 'the hand of God / a Catholic thing'
jokes.setup: Mac startles Trevor and assumes a fighting stance; Trevor asks about his training
jokes.punchline: Mac lists three legitimate martial arts; Frank counters with 'more of a Catholic thing going on... the hand of God' — presenting religion as a fighting style
jokes.explanation: Frank's 'hand of God' as a fighting discipline is very funny — the casual equivalence of faith to martial arts, and the specificity of 'Catholic' (not just religious) makes it feel grounded and strange simultaneously. Character-perfect for both Mac (the action movie wannabe) and Frank (the street-level survivor).

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You see, you thought you all could get together and play your little games, have some fun, you know, invite some geeks to the ball, swap some stories, have a laugh. Ha-ha-ha-ha-ha! But you took it a little too far... when you gave an inside-trading tip to my friend Mac, didn't you, Trevor?

jokes.text: Ruby receives a call from the Waitress — but doesn't know her name is 'Waitress' and keeps asking 'Who? Who?' as the Waitress insists on being called her name
jokes.setup: The Waitress calls Ruby's phone looking for Charlie; Ruby doesn't know who she is
jokes.punchline: The Waitress insists 'Because my name is not Waitress' — but Ruby literally has no name for her, and the audience knows the show has never given her one either
jokes.explanation: This is one of the funniest jokes in the episode and a genuine piece of meta-craft. The show has called her 'the Waitress' for years — she has no name in the narrative. When Ruby asks 'Who?' it breaks the fourth wall just enough: the audience is in on the joke that this character literally has no name. 'Because my name is not Waitress' is a great character moment for the Waitress who is finally asserting identity, and the humor is rich because we know the audience doesn't know her name either. Layered, original, and deeply show-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What was the context? Wrestling. It's wrestling. We're oiled up and wrestling. What is so hard to understand about this?!

jokes.text: Ruby's reaction to the Waitress: 'Look, I don't... (mocking): Ha, ha, ha, ha, ugh!' — dismissively mocking the Waitress's concern before hanging up
jokes.setup: The Waitress is urgently explaining she needs her bike back or she'll lose her job
jokes.punchline: Ruby (a wealthy person) dismissively mocks the working-class urgency with cartoonish laughter before hanging up
jokes.explanation: The class-contempt joke works in context but Ruby isn't established enough for her cruelty to land with full force. The mocking laugh is a little on-the-nose. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Charlie, look, I don't know what's been going on, but if you think you can make it stop, I need your help. I want you back in my life... I need you.

jokes.text: Dennis realizes: without Charlie doing his insane protective stalking, the Waitress's life will fall apart — and she'll show up at the worst possible moment
jokes.setup: Dennis and Frank are watching the Taft trap unfold
jokes.punchline: The ironic revelation that Charlie's creepy stalking was actually keeping the Waitress's life running — the absence of his obsession creates chaos
jokes.explanation: A smart structural callback — the list of Charlie's creepy 'helpful' behaviors from the opening now pays off as an ironic twist. The joke is that Charlie's obsession, while disturbing, was genuinely protective. The Waitress needs her stalker. This is good dark sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I was using you. That's why I kissed you in front of the waitress. That's why I banged you a bunch of times, just to make the waitress jealous... You know what you were acting like? A stupid little rich slut. And that's all that you are.

jokes.text: Frank tries to decode 'Charlie's chicken scratch' list of stalking tasks — including 'putting rat poison in her shampoo' — and Dennis says 'If he puts rat poison in her hair, put rat poison in her hair'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to replicate Charlie's stalker care-tasks from an illegible list
jokes.punchline: The list apparently includes putting rat poison in the Waitress's shampoo. Dennis's response: just follow the list.
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark escalation of the opening joke. Charlie claimed he put VITAMINS in her shampoo — now we learn his list actually says rat poison. Dennis's total moral indifference ('if he puts rat poison in her hair, put rat poison in her hair') is a great Dennis line. The callback reveals Charlie's self-serving reframing and Dennis's sociopathy simultaneously. Very good dark comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: She says no to a man, for years, like, ten years. That's what a real woman does, okay?

jokes.text: The Waitress calls Dennis demanding to know if Charlie stole her bike; Dennis: 'Who? Who?! Just say Waitress!'
jokes.setup: The Waitress calls Dennis and presumably gives her name
jokes.punchline: Dennis can't identify her either and blurts out 'Just say Waitress!' — confirming that everyone, including her acquaintances, only knows her as the Waitress
jokes.explanation: The running gag about the Waitress having no name pays off again here — now Dennis, who presumably knows her, also can't identify her by name and snaps 'Just say Waitress!' The irony that the person she's calling for help doesn't know her name either is both funny and oddly poignant. The parallel construction with the Ruby scene makes it a proper running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Guess Charlie had the cruelest intentions of all, huh?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'This bitch is driving me nuts' — referring to the Waitress calling him for help while he's managing Charlie's crisis
jokes.setup: Dennis is managing multiple crisis phone calls
jokes.punchline: He refers to the person he's supposed to be helping as 'this bitch' in a moment of pure exasperation
jokes.explanation: Minor Dennis exasperation beat. Works in context but isn't particularly crafted — it's just Dennis being Dennis in a low-stakes way.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Uh, I don't think there's 50 feet in this room, so...

jokes.text: Frank apparently breaks into the Waitress's apartment; she screams; Frank yells
jokes.setup: Frank has been tasked with doing Charlie's list of 'helpful' tasks for the Waitress, including accessing her home
jokes.punchline: The mutual screaming (Waitress screams at Frank, Frank yells back) implies Frank broke in and terrified her — presented as a routine task
jokes.explanation: Physical gag that works better visually. The screaming mutual shock is a standard break-in comedy beat, elevated slightly by the context — Frank is doing this as an act of 'kindness' on Charlie's behalf.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't think there's 50 feet in this room, so...

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: I'll go down the hall. Okay. I'll see you tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: All right, well, that's fine. From a distance, though.

jokes.text: Charlie tells Ruby there's a woman in the building who is 'the love of his life' — before the Waitress herself bursts in screaming at him
jokes.setup: Charlie is having a tender moment with Ruby and confesses his feelings for another woman
jokes.punchline: The Waitress immediately arrives — perfectly timed — to scream at Charlie about being poisoned, completely undermining the romantic moment
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — Charlie's romantic confession is immediately punctured by the reality of his relationship with the Waitress (hostile and chaotic). The timing payoff is satisfying.

jokes.text: The Waitress accuses Charlie of poisoning her; Charlie says he's been with Ruby ('I-I've been with her the last couple days'); the Waitress snaps at Ruby 'Oh, shut up, bitch!'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to defend himself with Ruby as his alibi
jokes.punchline: Ruby politely confirms, and the Waitress — angry and probably partially poisoned — instantly turns on her: 'Oh, shut up, bitch!'
jokes.explanation: The Waitress turning on a stranger for the crime of being calm and helpful is a good dark beat. It shows how Charlie's world has contaminated even the innocent Ruby. Quick and effective.

jokes.text: Charlie introduces Ruby to the Waitress as 'my girlfriend' — a beat of pure silence/shock
jokes.setup: The Waitress is mid-rage about being poisoned
jokes.punchline: Charlie, completely calmly, introduces Ruby as 'my girlfriend' — the first time he's ever been in this position — and the Waitress is dumbstruck
jokes.explanation: One of the most emotionally resonant jokes in the episode, which is what makes it so effective. Charlie simply saying 'She's my girlfriend' — two words that in context demolish a decade of unrequited obsession — is perfectly economical. The silence that follows (the Waitress's reaction, 'Oh my God') is the punchline. It earns 8+ for the structural perfection: maximum story development, minimum words, maximum impact. Only Charlie could deliver this, and only in this moment.

jokes.text: Mac and Dee wrestling Trevor in an oiled-up grappling session that escalates into Dee accidentally hitting Trevor and all three tumbling
jokes.setup: Mac teaches Trevor his fighting moves, which apparently require both parties to be 'oiled up'
jokes.punchline: The sequence escalates into genuine chaos — Dee yelling, grunting, someone getting 'clocked,' Trevor calling them 'out of control'
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that works better visually. The fact that the oiled-up wrestling is used as evidence against Trevor later is a good structural plant. In transcript form it reads as chaotic but functional.

jokes.text: Trevor invites the whole gang to a party at the estate despite everything — 'He's practically family'
jokes.setup: Mac, Dee, and Charlie have just behaved chaotically at Trevor's property
jokes.punchline: Trevor invites them all to a formal estate party — which the audience now knows (from Dennis's theory) is the setup for public humiliation
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is doing most of the work here. We know what the invitation means; the gang doesn't. 'He's practically family' about Mac is a small nice touch given Mac's uncle died in Taft's molten steel.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I should've known better, 'cause I'm practically a Taft myself. My uncle's probably built into the foundation of this place.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to claim belonging at the Taft estate
jokes.punchline: His claim to belonging is that his uncle died in their industrial accident and is probably literally embedded in their building — presented as a point of pride
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best lines in the episode. The callback to the uncle's death pays off perfectly — Mac's grotesque class aspiration expressed as 'my dead uncle is literally in your walls' as a form of belonging claim. The image of an industrial accident victim 'built into the foundation' is darkly poetic and very Sunny. Scores 8+ because it's a great callback, perfectly economical, and 100% Mac-specific in its delusional class striving.

jokes.text: Trevor seats Mac and Dee with 'some of my frat brothers' guests' — clearly the equivalent of the kids' table — then walks away with his actual friends
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee expect to be seated with Trevor at the party
jokes.punchline: Trevor politely but clearly demotes them to the loser section — the audience understands this is the beginning of the humiliation
jokes.explanation: The social snub is clear and well-executed. The dramatic irony (Mac and Dee don't get it yet) carries the moment. The 'we'll meet you after' response is a good oblivious beat.

jokes.text: Mac's response to being sidelined: 'At least we can make fun of these dorks all night long, right? That'll be fun. Geeks!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee have been sat with the undesirable guests
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately defaults to making himself feel better by calling the people around him 'dorks' and 'geeks' — not realizing he's the dork
jokes.explanation: Mac's obliviousness and reflexive bullying as a coping mechanism is well-characterized. 'Geeks!' shouted into the room is a funny image. The irony is obvious but well-deployed.

jokes.text: Dee realizes Trevor is 'doing to us what I like to do to Charlie and the waitress' — the gang recognizes themselves as the marks
jokes.setup: Mac is about to settle in and mock the other guests
jokes.punchline: Dee has a moment of self-awareness: she recognizes the game because she plays it herself — the gang are the butt of the joke
jokes.explanation: The moment of self-recognition is well-written — it confirms Dennis's theory and delivers the thematic point of the episode (the gang are always the worst people, until they're not). The irony that Dee recognizes it because she does it herself is sharp and character-specific.

jokes.text: The video footage of Mac and Dee fighting/wrestling Trevor is played to the entire party — the crowd laughs at their footage of Mac and Dee wrestling oiled up
jokes.setup: Trevor's humiliation plan is revealed — he's been filming the gang the whole time
jokes.punchline: The collected footage is played publicly; the oiled-up wrestling is apparently the highlight
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the wrestling setup works well — the oiled-up footage being the pièce de résistance of the humiliation reel is exactly right. Structural satisfaction in the callback.

jokes.text: Dennis's counter-gambit: plays a recording of Trevor giving Mac an insider trading tip while they were 'oiled up and wrestling'
jokes.setup: The Tafts think they've won and are humiliating the gang publicly
jokes.punchline: Dennis reveals he has been filming everything too ('If you're in my room, you're always being filmed. It's true. It's his thing. It's kind of creepy.') — and uses it to threaten SEC action
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Dennis films everything in his room (normalized as 'his thing, kind of creepy, but...') is an excellent Dennis character note that pays off structurally. 'If you're in my room, you're always being filmed' is terrifying and funny. The specific detail that the insider tip came during oiled-up wrestling is great contextual comedy.

jokes.text: Dennis's counter-scheme: 'You're not the only ones who know how to play these games' — arriving with a dramatic plan nobody else understands yet
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are reeling from being humiliated; Dennis appears with mysterious confidence
jokes.punchline: Dennis materializes with a vague but ominous declaration that he 'has a thing' — perfectly in character as the gang's self-appointed schemer
jokes.explanation: Setup beat more than a standalone joke. Dennis's smug counter-scheme entrance is in character but the joke is primarily in what follows, not in this line itself.

jokes.text: 'If you're in my room, you're always being filmed. It's true. It's his thing, it's kind of creepy, but...'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains how he got the incriminating footage
jokes.punchline: Mac casually confirms that Dennis films everyone in his room as a matter of routine — 'kind of creepy, but...' — and trails off, normalizing it completely
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'but...' after 'kind of creepy' is perfect — Mac was going to defend it and simply couldn't find the justification. The normalizing of Dennis's surveillance as just 'his thing' is deeply unsettling and deeply funny, especially in a crowd context. 'It's true' as the opening confirmation from Mac is excellent. This is exactly the kind of dark-casual line that makes Sunny great — delivered to a room of horrified wealthy people. Scores 8+ for character integration and the perfect trailing non-defense.

jokes.text: Trevor defending the insider trading: 'This is taken out of context.' Dennis: 'What was the context?' Trevor: 'Wrestling. It's wrestling. We're oiled up and wrestling. What is so hard to understand about this?!'
jokes.setup: Trevor tries to explain away the footage of him committing insider trading
jokes.punchline: His context defense is 'we were wrestling and oiled up' — which is somehow supposed to make a securities violation more innocent
jokes.explanation: 'What is so hard to understand about this?!' is a great closer — Trevor's indignation that people don't understand why oiled wrestling makes insider trading acceptable is perfectly absurd. The escalating frustration in his defense is well-structured.

jokes.text: Charlie's breakup speech to Ruby: 'You slept with me almost instantly. And by the way, a quality woman doesn't do that. She says no to a man, for years, like, ten years. That's what a real woman does.'
jokes.setup: Ruby is devastated that Charlie is leaving her; Charlie explains why she's not worthy
jokes.punchline: Charlie's ideal of a 'quality woman' is one who refuses him for TEN YEARS — an exact description of the Waitress's behavior — and he's presenting it as a virtue
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best Charlie jokes in the series. Charlie has so completely internalized his rejection by the Waitress that rejection itself has become his love language — 'she says no to a man, for YEARS, like TEN YEARS' is an exact description of his obsession reframed as a masculine ideal. It's simultaneously delusional, devastating, funny, and psychologically precise. The 'ten years' specificity is perfect. Only Charlie Kelly could say this. It's the dark heart of Charlie's character revealed as comedy. Scores among the top jokes of the episode because it's character-defining, structurally elegant, deeply original, and quotable.

jokes.text: Charlie to Ruby: 'You know what you were acting like? A stupid little rich slut. And that's all that you are.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just delivered his 'quality woman' speech
jokes.punchline: He punctuates it with an utterly vicious insult delivered with complete sincerity and calm
jokes.explanation: The viciousness lands because of the contrast with Charlie's usual obliviousness — he becomes briefly and terrifyingly lucid. But it's a less sophisticated joke than the preceding 'ten years' speech. Works as a dark button to the scene.

jokes.text: Ruby cries 'How can you do this to me?' — Charlie: 'Are you still talking? Go away, dumb-dumb. Go run and hide. Go from me.'
jokes.setup: Ruby is visibly devastated and emotional
jokes.punchline: Charlie dismisses her tears with 'Are you still talking? Go away, dumb-dumb' — delivered with complete disinterest
jokes.explanation: 'Go away, dumb-dumb' is very Charlie — childlike vocabulary deployed with adult cruelty. 'Go from me' is a weird, slightly archaic phrasing that sounds like Charlie's particular grammar. Good character voice.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Guess Charlie had the cruelest intentions of all, huh?'
jokes.setup: Everyone watches Charlie walk away from Ruby
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the episode's thesis as a wry one-liner — referencing both the film 'Cruel Intentions' (his earlier reference) and the irony that Charlie, the innocent, turned out to be the most ruthless player
jokes.explanation: A great closing button to the episode's plot. The callback to 'Cruel Intentions' pays off with a thematic twist — Charlie is the cruelest player of all, unintentionally. The phrasing is clean and quotable. Near-perfect economy for a wrap-up line.

jokes.text: The Waitress tells Charlie she's been thinking about the restraining order — Charlie's face lights up — she says she's NOT getting rid of it, just reducing from 100 to 50 feet
jokes.setup: Charlie has just reunited with the Waitress and she says she's been 'thinking about the restraining order' — implying she might lift it
jokes.punchline: She's reducing it from 100 to 50 feet. Charlie responds: 'Awesome! Okay. I can work with that.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The setup is a perfect fake-out — 'I've been thinking about the restraining order' genuinely sounds like it might be progress. The punchline 'reducing from 100 to 50 feet' is a beautiful deflation that's also a tiny win for Charlie. 'Awesome! I can work with that' is the perfect Charlie response — total acceptance of the crumbs he's given. The restraining order as a unit of love in this relationship is brilliantly dark. Scores 8+ for structure, character specificity, and the genuine emotional resonance underneath the comedy.

jokes.text: The Waitress points out there isn't 50 feet in the room — Charlie offers to go down the hall
jokes.setup: The restraining order is being observed; they're in the same small room
jokes.punchline: The practical impossibility of maintaining 50 feet in an apartment means Charlie has to go down the hall — and he cheerfully accepts this
jokes.explanation: The final escalation of the restraining order gag — not only is 50 feet a terrible 'win,' the room doesn't even accommodate it, so their 'closeness' is immediately separated again. Charlie going down the hall and looking forward to seeing her tomorrow 'from a distance' is the perfect dark-sweet ending note. The last line 'From a distance, though' is excellent.

tmdb_overview: Charlie and Dee become romantically involved with two members of a wealthy family, which arouses jealousy in Mac, Dennis and Frank.
